consensual non-monogamy: Having more than one romantic or sexual relationship, with everyone knowing and agreeing.
ethical non-monogamy: Having more than one romantic or sexual relationship, with everyone knowing and agreeing.
non-monogamy: Not limiting yourself to one romantic or sexual partner.
cnm: Short for consensual non-monogamy: more than one relationship, with everyone knowing and agreeing.
enm: Short for ethical non-monogamy: more than one relationship, with everyone knowing and agreeing.
polyamory: Having more than one loving relationship at a time, with everyone's knowledge.
polyamorous: Open to more than one loving relationship at a time, with everyone's knowledge.
monogamy: Having one romantic and sexual partner at a time.
relationship anarchy: Building each relationship your own way, without ranking partners above friends.
solo polyamory: Having several relationships while keeping your own independent life as the base.
swinging: Committed couples who have sex with other people, often together and socially.
polycule: The whole network of people linked through their relationships.
hierarchical: Set up so some relationships come first and get more say.
veto: The power to make a partner end or block another relationship.
couple privilege: When an existing couple's comfort always wins over a newer partner's needs.
compersion: Feeling happy because your partner is happy with someone else.
new relationship energy: The rush of excitement and obsession at the start of a new relationship.
nre: Short for new relationship energy: the excited rush at the start of something new.
kitchen table polyamory: Everyone is friendly enough to sit around one table together.
parallel polyamory: Partners' other partners have little or no contact with each other.
garden party polyamory: Partners' other partners are friendly at events but not close.
mono-normativity: The belief that having one partner is the only normal way to do relationships.
amatonormativity: The belief that everyone should want one central romantic relationship.
heteronormativity: The belief that being straight is the normal, default way to be.
chosen family: People you pick as family, whether or not you are related.
fluid bonding: Agreeing to have sex with a specific partner without condoms or other barriers.
coercion: Pushing, pressuring or tricking someone into saying yes.
autonomy: Your right to run your own life and make your own choices.
bodily autonomy: Your right to decide what happens to your own body.
accountability: Owning the harm you caused and working to repair it.
nonviolent communication: A four-step way to speak honestly without blaming: what happened, how you feel, what you need, what you ask.
nvc: Short for Nonviolent Communication: say what happened, how you feel, what you need, and what you ask.
empathic listening: Listening to understand how someone feels, not to argue or fix.
emotional bid: Any small attempt to connect, like a comment, a touch or a look.
emotional intelligence: Noticing feelings, yours and other people's, and handling them well.
self-regulation: Calming yourself down when feelings run high.
co-regulation: Calming down with the help of another person.
dysregulation: When your feelings or body are too stirred up to think clearly.
window of tolerance: The zone where you feel steady enough to think and talk.
polyvagal theory: An idea about how your body's alarm system switches between calm, fight-or-flight and shutdown.
nervous system: Your body's wiring that controls stress, calm and reactions.
attachment theory: The idea that early care shapes how safe you feel getting close to people.
attachment style: Your usual pattern of getting close to people or pulling away.
secure attachment: Feeling safe being close to people and safe being apart.
nested security: Feeling safe on several levels: in yourself, in each relationship and in the wider group.
emotional caretaking: Taking on the job of fixing someone else's feelings for them.
sti: A sexually transmitted infection: an infection passed on through sex.
prep: A medicine taken ahead of time that prevents getting HIV.
pep: Emergency medicine taken soon after a possible exposure to prevent HIV.
u=u: Undetectable equals untransmittable: someone on working HIV treatment cannot pass it on through sex.
viral load: How much of a virus is in someone's blood.
undetectable: So little virus in the blood that tests cannot find it.
barrier method: Something that blocks fluids during sex, like a condom or dental dam.
harm reduction: Making something safer instead of demanding people stop doing it.
stigma: Shame or judgement that people attach to something.
cisgender: Your gender matches the sex you were given at birth.
transgender: Your gender is different from the sex you were given at birth.
nonbinary: A gender that is not simply man or woman.
intersex: Born with a body that does not fit the usual boxes of male or female.
gender identity: Your own inner sense of your gender.
gender expression: How you show gender through clothes, voice, style and behaviour.
gender-affirming: Supporting a person in living as their gender.
hormone therapy: Taking hormones, often to bring the body in line with someone's gender.
perimenopause: The years leading up to menopause, when hormones start to shift.
menopause: When periods stop for good and hormone levels drop.
ssris: A common type of antidepressant medicine.
pelvic floor: The muscles at the bottom of your pelvis that hold up your bladder and bowel.
anorgasmia: Not being able to reach orgasm.
spontaneous desire: Wanting sex out of the blue.
responsive desire: Wanting sex after things start to feel good or close.
dual control model: The idea that turn-ons work like a gas pedal and turn-offs like a brake.
sexual excitation system: Your gas pedal: everything that turns you on.
sexual inhibition system: Your brakes: everything that turns you off or holds you back.
arousal non-concordance: When your body reacts but your mind is not turned on, or the other way round.
spectatoring: Watching and judging yourself during sex instead of feeling it.
embodiment: Being present in your body and noticing what you feel.
mindfulness: Paying calm attention to right now.
sensate focus: A slow, step-by-step touching exercise with no goal except noticing how it feels.
biopsychosocial: Looking at body, mind and life situation together.
non-pathologizing: Not treating a difference as a sickness.
pathologizing: Treating a difference as a sickness.
desire discrepancy: When partners want sex at different rates.
trauma-informed: Done with care for people who have been through painful experiences.
aasect: A US group that trains and certifies sex therapists and educators.
sexual fluidity: When who you are attracted to shifts over time.
asexuality: Feeling little or no sexual attraction to anyone.
asexual: Feeling little or no sexual attraction to anyone.
aromantic: Feeling little or no romantic attraction to anyone.
split attraction model: The idea that romantic pull and sexual pull are two separate things.
erasure: Acting as if a group of people does not exist.
allyship: Backing a group you are not part of through what you do, not just what you say.
fetishization: Treating a person as a turn-on because of a label, not as a whole person.
intersectionality: How parts of who you are, like race, gender and disability, combine to shape your life.
marginalized: Pushed to the edges and given less power or respect.
systemic: Built into rules, laws and institutions, not just one person's actions.
desexualization: Treating someone as if they have no sexual feelings.
neurodivergent: Having a brain that works differently from what is seen as typical, like autism or ADHD.
neurodivergence: Natural differences in how brains work, like autism or ADHD.
neurotypical: Having a brain that works in the way most people expect.
executive function: The brain skills for planning, starting tasks and keeping track of time.
hypersensitivity: Feeling touch, sound or light much more strongly than most people.
double empathy problem: The idea that autistic and non-autistic people misread each other both ways.
colonialism: When one country takes over another and forces its rules and beliefs on the people.
patriarchal: Set up so that men hold most of the power.
polyandry: One woman married to more than one man.
reproductive justice: The right to have children, not have children, and raise them in safety.
eugenics: The abusive idea of controlling who is allowed to have children.
ncii: Sharing someone's private sexual images without their permission.
cyberstalking: Using phones or the internet to follow, watch or scare someone.
aftercare: Checking in and caring for each other after something intense.
kink: Sexual interests outside the mainstream that people enjoy by agreement.
bdsm: Agreed play with power, restraint or sensation between consenting adults.
safe word: An agreed word that stops everything right away.
neuroplasticity: The brain's ability to change and build new habits.
codependency: Losing yourself in looking after someone else's problems.
compulsivity: Feeling driven to keep doing something even when it causes harm.
hypervigilance: Being on constant alert for danger.
ambiguous loss: A loss with no clear ending, like someone who is still here but changed.
stonewalling: Shutting down and refusing to respond during a conflict.
de-escalation: Bringing the heat of a conflict down.
love bombing: Flooding someone with attention and gifts early on, as a way to gain control over them.
trauma bond: A strong pull toward someone who hurts you and then is kind, over and over.
trauma bonds: Strong pulls toward someone who hurts you and then is kind, over and over.
self-efficacy: Believing that you are able to do something.
mirror neurons: Brain cells that fire when you watch someone act, as if you were doing it yourself.
emotional contagion: Feelings spreading from one person to another, like a yawn.
psychological safety: Feeling safe to speak up, ask questions or make mistakes without being punished.
growth mindset: Believing you can get better at things with effort and practice.
fixed mindset: Believing your abilities are set and cannot change.
repair attempt: Any small move that lowers the tension during a fight, like a joke or an apology.
repair attempts: Small moves that lower the tension during a fight, like a joke or an apology.
gridlocked: So stuck that you cannot even talk about it without getting hurt or angry.
flooding: When stress overwhelms your body so much that you cannot think or listen.
conscious uncoupling: Ending a relationship on purpose, with care and respect.
anticipatory grief: Feeling the loss of something before it has actually ended.
post-traumatic growth: Growing in good ways after going through something very hard.
money scripts: Hidden beliefs about money that you picked up early in life.
financial abuse: Controlling someone by controlling their money.
interdependence: Relying on each other while each still having your own life.
dopamine: A brain chemical tied to reward and wanting more.
oxytocin: A brain chemical tied to bonding and trust.
prefrontal cortex: The front part of the brain used for planning and good judgement.
somatic: To do with the body and what it feels.
affirmations: Short, kind statements you repeat to yourself.
visualization: Picturing something in your mind as practice for doing it.
habit stacking: Attaching a new habit to one you already do.
implementation intentions: A plan that says exactly when and where you will do something.
scarcity mindset: The belief that there is not enough to go around.
heart coherence: A steady, smooth heart rhythm linked with calm feelings.
intermittent reinforcement: Rewards that come unpredictably, which makes a habit very hard to break.
fawn: Trying to please someone to stay safe.
triggers: Things that set off an old alarm or painful feeling.
infidelity: Breaking an agreement to be faithful. Cheating.
renegotiation: Talking an agreement through again and updating it.
hierarchy: A ranking where some relationships come before others.
sliding scale: A price that goes down if you earn less.
sliding-scale: Priced lower if you earn less.
